Operation Co-Pilot: redesigning the Royal Mail field PDA

A rugged, glove-friendly navigation HUD for the Personal Digital Assistant (PDA) that Royal Mail drivers carry, designed from 12 field failures I lived and observed.

Role: lead UX researcher, interaction designer and product strategist. Timeline: November 2025 to October 2026, an independent initiative alongside my own rounds. Tools: Figma, FigJam, contextual inquiry, auto-ethnography, benchmarking. This is an independent project, not affiliated with Royal Mail, and uses no internal screens or data.

Summary

Royal Mail’s roughly 85,000 delivery workers use rugged handheld PDAs. The software handles compliance, legal tracking, barcode verification and meter-accurate delivery points reliably. Its interface, though, ignores the physical, cognitive and spatial reality of a round.

As an active driver with an MSc in UX Design, I audited it across my own rounds from November 2025 to October 2026. On the same parcel manifest, a modern route optimiser beat the PDA’s own time estimate on almost every round: about 2 hours against 2.5 on some, and about 1.5 against 3 on others. I documented 12 field failures and designed a HUD that answers each one.

How I researched it

Because I am an insider, I triangulated my own experience so the findings are not just my frustrations.

  • Benchmark: timed Circuit on Google Maps against the PDA’s own time estimate for the same manifests, across my rounds. Circuit was faster on almost every round, by about 20% on some (2 hours against 2.5) and by up to half on others (1.5 hours against 3).
  • Contextual inquiry: talked with and observed 12 peer drivers, especially new drivers, across rural van, high-density walking and commercial multi-drop rounds.
  • Auto-ethnography: logged friction, cognitive load spikes and failures on my own rounds from November 2025 to October 2026.
  • Heuristic review: Jakob’s Law, visibility of system status, recognition over recall and Fitts’s Law.

What to keep: the PDA’s meter-level delivery-point accuracy beats consumer maps, and its scanning is reliable. Consumer apps win on route optimisation, so the redesign adds that without losing these strengths.

The problem at a glance

Designing for the brutal street

GlovesWinter gloves remove fine motor control, so small targets fail.
Rain and glareDroplets cause ghost touches and break pinch gestures. Sun washes out grey text.
Motion hazardsDrivers glance at the screen while walking uneven drives with heavy parcels.
Failing mountsHire vans often lack holders and suction mounts fall off. The PDA ends up in a cup holder or on the seat, far from the driver’s sightline.

The 12 field failures

Routing and spatial blind spots

1. Rigid routingStops follow postcode sequence, not roads, forcing U-turns and backtracking. Many drivers fall back on Circuit.
2. Navigation blind spotThe active map isolates one stop. The overview map sits on a separate screen, so drivers cannot see neighbouring drops while navigating.
3. Proximity paradox#12 and #17 can be next door, yet the route sends you away and back. Hidden neighbours block opportunistic bundling.
4. Locked zoom and gesturesThe camera stays zoomed in whatever the speed. Zooming out needs a pinch that fails with gloves or rain.
5. Reroute latencyAfter a missed turn the screen takes around 5 seconds to load, then keeps showing the old directions for a while before it offers a new route from the way you are now heading.

Physical and cognitive friction

6. Lost headingThe map does not show which way to set off. Its arrow just points straight ahead, so you have to drive a few metres to find out if it is the right way, and turn around if it is not.
7. Parking blind spotThe arrival screen hides where the next stop is, so drivers park facing the wrong way and need multi-point turns.
8. House number amnesiaAt arrival, traffic and parking wipe the number from memory, and the map shows route lines instead of text.
9. Heads-down hazardWith the PDA off its mount, the type is too small to read at a glance.

System and data fragility

10. Static data trapThe PDA is accurate to the metre, but it can send you to a back porch with no access when the main entrance is on a different street. Wrong entrances and locked gates cannot be flagged, so every later driver repeats the error.
11. Rigid manifestA parcel found in the van or pushed mid-route means restarting progress or hunting through lists.
12. Zombie Wi-FiDepot Wi-Fi is weak, and the PDA clings to it while the route is being built. Wi-Fi cannot be switched off, so the route stalls until you move out of range, even though 4G works fine.

Design principles from the field

Each principle answers a stressor: black, white and amber for glare, 32pt+ type for the cup-holder glance, 56 to 72px targets for gloves, and every key action in the bottom thumb zone.

Benchmark and competitive review

MetricNative PDAModern pattern (Circuit, Google Maps)
Manifest time2.5 to 3 hours (PDA estimate)1.5 to 2 hours (20 to 50% less)
RoutingRigid postcode sequence, U-turnsOptimised path, continuous flow
MappingStatic close-up, isolated stop, gesture lockVelocity zoom, multi-stop pins, tap to reorder
KnowledgeNone, errors persistDriver pin-drops and arrival notes
NetworkSticky Wi-Fi stalls syncThroughput-based failover

Jakob’s Law explains why this matters: drivers already know these patterns from consumer apps, so adoption would be fast. Building on that, I suggest the PDA could show nearby stops as pins, let drivers re-order stops straight from the map, and show access notes left by other drivers on arrival.

The redesign

Solution 1: one HUD instead of two screens

  • Peripheral pins: upcoming stops sit on the active map. Tap #17 beside #12 to bundle it into one walk.
  • Velocity-based zoom: the camera pulls out on straights and tightens at junctions. A Macro/Micro button replaces pinch. Dragging enters explore mode and the map re-centres after a few seconds.
  • Trajectory and heading lock: a dotted line past the current stop shows the next heading, so you park facing the exit. The heading freezes on arrival.
  • Arrival card: within about 100 metres a black-on-amber “NUMBER 42” banner locks to the top, readable from a cup holder.

Solution 2: frontline pin drop

A floating Correct Access button opens three huge presets: wrong gate or wall, true entrance on a GPS-suggested street, or drop a pin here. No typing. The next driver gets a geofenced warning banner, which also gives agency and seasonal staff veteran knowledge on day one.

PLAY

Fix a wrong address in 3 seconds

Tap the glowing buttons on the phone and beat the clock. This is the redesigned flow, and the score is just for fun, not research data.

TIME0.0 s

Solution 3: a manifest and network that bend

  • Smart slot-in: scanning a stray parcel suggests the nearest fit, such as Stop 12B, with a second option to append to the end of the route.
  • Delta pre-caching: the two likeliest detours are cached ahead, with a design target of rerouting in under 500 ms.
  • Network failover: below about 2 Mbps the app moves traffic to 4G or 5G, with a one-tap Force Cellular override.

Business value

85,000 workers × 0.5 hours = 42,500 hours a day. This is a projection, not a measurement. It assumes only 30 minutes saved per day, the smallest gap I saw on my own rounds, and is an upper bound because not every worker has a comparable round.

Beyond time: less fuel and fewer backtracked miles, faster seasonal onboarding, fewer mis-sorts and failed first deliveries, fewer “lost parcel” calls from bad delivery points, and less daily frustration for drivers.

42,500projected hours saved daily (85,000 drivers × 0.5 h)
20–50%less route time than the PDA estimate in my benchmark
Fewer milesless backtracking and U-turns; emissions impact still to be quantified
Day-one readycrowdsourced access notes help agency and seasonal drivers

Graphic 8. Projected business impact, based on my benchmark and a conservative assumption.

Rationale and next steps

Problem statement and how-might-we questions

The PDA verifies parcels reliably but sequences a round like a database, not like a person walking a street. On the same manifest, my benchmark showed the native sequence taking up to twice as long as an optimised route.

  • How might we show a driver the whole neighbourhood while navigating a single stop?
  • How might we make the next address glanceable with gloved hands and eyes on traffic?
  • How might we turn a driver’s local knowledge into shared data in under 3 seconds?

Who I designed for

Three archetypes from the 12 drivers I shadowed.

Rural van round

Long gaps, frequent dismounts. Needs heading lock, parking feedforward and reliable data (failures 6, 7, 12).

High-density walking round

Dozens of adjacent doors. Needs proximity bundling and number clarity (failures 1, 3, 8).

Commercial multi-drop

Gates, loading bays, late parcels. Needs access notes and mid-route injection (failures 10, 11).

Design decisions and trade-offs

  • Presets over typing. Gloves make keyboards unusable. The cost is less nuance, so add an “Other” option and consider voice notes later.
  • Low-opacity proximity pins. They give awareness without clutter. Risk: mis-taps, so pins keep a 56px minimum target.
  • Crowdsourced access notes. Fast knowledge sharing, but unverified data can mislead. Proposal: promote a note after two drivers confirm it.
  • Cellular failover. Depends on device management policy and data allowances, so it needs IT sign-off.

Validation plan and next steps

Status: high-fidelity prototype, not yet tested with drivers. Next, run moderated tests with 5 to 8 drivers wearing winter gloves, measuring time to confirm an address, glance duration, error rate and SUS score. Replace projections with measured results as they arrive.

Scope, ethics and privacy

This is an independent project, not affiliated with Royal Mail, and it uses no internal screens or data. Location pins raise privacy questions, so the design logs addresses and access points, never individual driver tracking.

What I learned

The biggest wins came from small moments, like the second before a driver parks or the half-minute after returning to the cab. Designing for the worst conditions made the interface better for everyone.

Conclusion

The most useful enterprise design starts where the work happens. Combining formal UX method with years on the street let me find failures that office-bound research would miss, and turn them into a design and a business case.

Someone’s ahead: a cycle-safety marker for the Meadows

A small roadside display for Edinburgh’s busiest shared path that shows cyclists their speed and warns them of people around blind bends, tested with a cardboard prototype and a bike.

MSc coursework, Edinburgh Napier University (Design Dialogues), 2023. Individual project. Methods: semi-structured interviews, field observation, storyboarding, physical prototyping, on-site usability testing, a 5-second test, the System Usability Scale and an expert review. Participants gave written consent and are anonymised here.

The problem

The Meadows is one of Edinburgh’s favourite open spaces, and its paths are shared by walkers, runners, dog walkers and cyclists. People drift across the painted lines, and around bends a cyclist cannot see who is ahead. Shared paths matter: in one study, 36.1% of bicycle accidents happened on shared pedestrian and cycle paths, more than on dedicated cycle paths.

I cycle there myself, and once had to brake hard when someone stepped into the cycle lane without looking.

Understanding: interviews and observation

I combined two methods because what people say and what they do are different. I interviewed 5 people at the Meadows, aged 19 to 60, over two cold days, and spent time observing how people actually used the paths.

Lanes are blurryGroups, slow walkers being overtaken and children playing drift into the cycle lane, often without noticing.
Blind spotsPeople felt safe overall, but not at bends and junctions, especially by the busy café on the corner.
DistractionHeadphones and phones reduce awareness, for walkers and cyclists alike.
Fast e-bikesDelivery riders on powerful electric bikes were seen as the biggest danger.
Light, not noiseVisual alerts were preferred, as sound could disturb a quiet park.
A familiar ideaOne participant described speed displays she had seen in Belgium, which showed riders how fast they were going.

The concept

I first considered glowing lane markings, then chose a small display shaped like a milestone, so it blends into the park. A lidar sensor would detect people in the lane ahead, and the display would use colours everyone already knows from traffic lights: green for go, yellow for slow down, red for stop. It dims at night, lowers the speed limit in rain and ice when stopping distances grow, and runs on solar power.

Test 1: riding past a cardboard prototype

I took my bike and the prototype to the Meadows. Three participants rode past it, then answered questions about clarity, text size, icons and alerts.

Too small to read“I could only read it from close up.” The red was visible, but the text was not.
Wrong heightIt should sit at a cyclist’s eye level.
Looks like a gravestoneThe black box needed a friendlier form and more colour.
Confusing number“Is that the speed limit or my speed?”

I cut the screens down to the essential elements and redesigned them as four states.

Test 2: a 5-second test

A cyclist only gets a glance, so I showed three participants the screens for 5 seconds and asked what they remembered.

The wrong thing stuckOne participant remembered the speed, but the design needed them to notice STOP first.
Signs over words“Make the symbols bigger.” Icons were easier to take in than text.
Colours without meaningOne participant noticed three colours but did not have time to work out what they meant.

Evaluation

The same three participants rated the design on the System Usability Scale, with scores of 50, 82.5 and 80: an average of 70.8, just above the benchmark of 68. One participant was unsure how to fill in the form, which pulled the average down. A senior UX designer at an Edinburgh studio then reviewed the idea and suggested placing the display at eye level, bringing back glowing lane lines for night time, adding a gentle beep when someone steps into the lane, and making it solar-powered.

The final design

What testing showedWhat changed
People remembered the speed, not the instructionSLOW DOWN, THANK YOU and STOP became the largest element; speed moved below in white
Speed limit and current speed were confusedThe speed limit has its own screen with a ring, separate from the rider’s speed
Too many elements to take in at a glanceOne icon per screen, and two flashing icons only on STOP
Text unreadable from a distance, display too lowLarger type, and the display raised to a cyclist’s eye level

Reflection and next steps

  • Samples were small: 5 interviews, 3 riders and 3 people in the 5-second test. It took about 25 approaches to find 5 people willing to stop in the cold.
  • Most interviewees were walkers, because stopping cyclists is hard. Next time I would recruit cyclists in advance.
  • Rain destroyed the prototype during testing, and the 5-second test showed three screens at once, which may have been too much.
  • Next I would test the final screens at full size and real distance, with riders at different speeds and at night.

Why can’t users leave? Dark patterns in social media

An MSc research project on how social media design works against users’ control of their own settings, tested on Facebook, and whether small design fixes help.

MSc User Experience Design dissertation, Edinburgh Napier University, April 2024. Sole researcher and designer. Platform studied: Facebook. Methods: semi-structured interviews, cognitive walkthrough with think-aloud, thematic and task analysis, expert review, focus group and prototype testing. Tools: Figma, Microsoft Teams, Turboscribe.

0 of 8found the account deactivation page
0 of 8found the recycle bin for deleted posts
2 of 8turned off all notifications
5 of 5completed all four tasks on my redesign

Summary

I asked eight regular social media users to complete six everyday tasks on Facebook, the platform I chose to experiment on, while thinking aloud, and found where the design works against them. I then redesigned the failed task flows in Figma and tested the result.

On the redesign, all five test participants completed all four tasks that most people had failed. Back on the real app, participants who had just used my prototype still could not find deactivation or the recycle bin, and only one of three found the ad settings. Knowing where settings are is not enough when the design resists you.

Research question: how do dark patterns in social media interfaces influence user behaviour and awareness, and what strategies can reduce their addictive effects?

What are dark patterns?

Dark patterns are interface designs that use what designers know about human behaviour to steer people toward actions that benefit the company, not the user. Harry Brignull coined the term in 2010, and Gray and colleagues (2018) later grouped the tricks by the strategy a designer uses. Picture a shop with a wide entrance and an exit hidden behind a maze of stairs.

They exist because attention is the currency of social media: more time in the app means more advertising revenue. Persuasive design is not always bad. Eyal’s Hooked model, which cycles through trigger, action, variable reward and investment, has also been used to help people build healthy habits. That tension is why I treated this as an ethics question as well as a usability one.

NaggingRepeated interruptions you can’t dismiss for good, such as a “Not now” prompt to turn on notifications with no “never” option. In my study: notification prompts popping up mid-task.
ObstructionMaking a task harder than it needs to be, like the “roach motel”: easy to get into, hard to get out of. In my study: deactivating the account (0 of 8 succeeded).
SneakingHiding or delaying information that matters to you. In my study: deleted posts quietly kept for 30 days in a hard-to-find bin.
Interface interferenceHighlighting some actions and burying others through hidden information, pre-selected options or false hierarchy. In my study: ads between tasks and key settings buried several levels deep.
Forced actionYou must do something to keep using a feature. Privacy “Zuckering” tricks you into sharing more data than you meant to. In my study: accept personalised ads or pay a monthly fee.
Patterns built for feedsInfinite scroll, autoplay, pull-to-refresh and endless recommendations keep you scrolling, and likes and followers build a sense of investment. I did not test these because my test account had no personalised feed.

Sources: Gray et al. (2018) taxonomy; Kelly and Burkell (2023) on privacy dark patterns; Monge Roffarello and De Russis (2022) on social media design.

How I researched it

My topic is social media as a whole, and I chose Facebook as the platform to experiment on: a long-established service whose decline is often linked to engagement-first design. I also included Marketplace tasks. To keep the data honest I:

  • Left the words “dark patterns” and “addiction” out of all participant materials, so I did not prime anyone. I asked about time spent instead.
  • Adapted the pre-task interview questions from published addiction questionnaires and reworded them to meet ethical standards.
  • Piloted the protocol. The pilot showed the tasks needed a think-aloud protocol.
  • Used a fresh account to remove personalisation, and obtained ethical approval and informed consent.
  • Triangulated interviews, think-aloud and screen recordings.

What I found

Participants described opening social media almost by reflex, often forgetting why they opened it. As one put it, “it’s not that I spent more time, it’s that I forget I spend time.” Boredom and fear of missing out were common triggers, and their own limits (time limits, uninstalling) were usually bypassed. None knew the term “dark patterns”, though they noticed hidden options.

Turning off notifications (2 of 8)The option sits at the bottom of a long list and many users did not know what “push notifications” meant. Obstruction and interface interference.
Deactivating the account (0 of 8)Adding another account is easy, but leaving is buried under Account Centre, then personal details. A “roach motel” pattern.
Deleting a post and finding the recycle bin (0 of 8)Deleted posts stay for 30 days and the bin hides inside the activity log. Sneaking and obfuscation.
Ad privacy settings (3 of 8)Choices were accept ads or pay a monthly fee, with vague wording, and the settings moved after choosing. Forced action and bait and switch.

The redesign

Rather than inventing a new app, I kept the long-form structure of the Facebook app and changed only what the findings pointed to, so any improvement could be attributed to those tweaks.

ProblemChange in the Figma prototype
No way to turn off all notificationsAdded a turn-off-all option and organised settings by where notifications come from, not each type
Deactivation hiddenMade Account Centre match the rest of the menu, relocated and relabelled deactivation, then added a menu shortcut after the expert review
Recycle bin buriedDirect route to the bin from settings, under the activity log
Ad preferences buriedMoved out of Account Centre into privacy and ad settings, reachable through Privacy Checkup, with a third option to use less information
Confusing wordingRenamed “Profile details” to “Personal details” after the expert review

Real app versus prototype

Same tasks and the same app structure. The top image in each pair is the real Facebook Android app, captured for this study with personal details covered. The bottom image is my Figma prototype.

More task flows: notifications and privacy preferences

These screens belong to Meta and appear here only to analyse the interface. The prototype is an unofficial study replica.

Evaluation

  • Expert review: a senior experience designer with an accessibility focus pushed for more prominent options, fewer steps, plain-language writing and confirmation steps. I made the changes listed above.
  • Focus group (5 participants): they debated whether companies or users carry the responsibility. Most sided with users, and one defended companies.
  • Task test: five participants used the prototype, and three then tried the same tasks on the real app.

The real finding is the third bar. Even with a recent look at where settings live, most people still failed on the real app, so this problem needs platform and policy change, not only user education. I still turned the findings into nine practical guidelines for users, such as using built-in focus tools, putting devices out of reach and demanding simpler settings.

Limitations

  • The study tests one platform, Facebook, so the findings may not carry over to services such as Instagram or TikTok.
  • The samples are small and student-heavy, with participants in their 20s and 30s. The results show patterns, not statistics.
  • Two participants appeared in both the research and the evaluation, and the prototype test was not a controlled experiment.
  • The fresh test account had no personalised feed, so autoplay and infinite scroll were not captured in the tasks.
  • It was my first time moderating a focus group, and it drifted off topic at times.
  • The work does not show lasting behaviour change, and it only touches the medical side of addiction.

What I would do next

Run a longer diary study of real use, recruit a wider and older sample, measure time on task, errors and SUS scores, and test with a personalised feed. This project also shaped my later work: the same toolkit of think-aloud, task analysis, triangulation and Figma prototypes is how I plan to validate my Royal Mail PDA redesign.

The Figma prototype and full appendices are available on request.

Fountain Flow: a playful app to control a relaxation fountain

A mobile app that lets people shape a fountain’s water flow, lights and sound from their phone, designed for calm, crowded public spaces.

MSc coursework, Edinburgh Napier University (Divergent Interaction). My individual work: the app’s UX and UI in Figma. It builds on our group’s Arduino fountain from an earlier project, where I ran the user interviews. Methods: interviews, persona, MoSCoW, journey mapping, divergent thinking, user flows, iteration and high-fidelity prototyping.

Where it started: our group’s Arduino fountain

Fountain Flow grew out of an earlier group project for the Divergent Interaction module, where four of us built the Harmonious Relaxation Fountain: a small working fountain that combines the sound of water with light and soft music to help people unwind. My part: I ran the user interviews, created the persona, the MoSCoW priorities and the journey map, helped build the fountain and made the project video.

Watch the fountain working ↗

What the interviews showed

I interviewed six students at Edinburgh Napier University about where they go to relax and how they feel near fountains.

Water calmsEveryone named the sound of water as what relaxed them. One said being near a fountain made them feel like a child again.
Neglect and safetyPeople disliked abandoned fountains, and worried that open fountains surprise children and older people.
Light divides opinionSome wanted lights only at night, one wanted them in the day too, and one wanted no lights at all, only soft music.
Keep it quietSoft music, not rock. One participant wanted a way to escape the noise of other tourists.

Diverging, then converging

Our first idea, for a sustainability brief, was a fountain powered by pedalling a bicycle. A small dynamo could not power the pump, and peer feedback questioned whether it was doable, so we converged on health and well-being, which the interviews supported.

The build was hard. Components failed, the buzzer weakened after water splashes, LEDs faltered and hot glue would not hold the stones. People controlled the finished fountain with four physical buttons, and we did not get to test it with real participants. In my individual coursework, I designed Fountain Flow to replace those buttons with an app.

The brief

The fountain from my team’s earlier Arduino project was inspired by natural waterfalls. One Arduino plays music and the other listens to the sound to drive the pump and the lights. My task was the app that controls it.

I set one goal: full control without touching a physical button, in a way that feels playful. A QR code on the fountain downloads the app and connects to that particular fountain, which can have its own features at its own location.

Who it is for

Sarah, 24A graphic design postgraduate from Vietnam studying in Edinburgh. Tech-savvy, relaxes near water, in parks and in cafes.
Pain pointsPublic spaces are noisy and crowded. She never has time to recharge. She dislikes neglected fountains and worries about their safety for children and people with disabilities.
NeedsCalm, open spaces. Lights and music that are carefully designed, not intrusive. Technology that creates a noise-free feel.

The intended audience is people aged 18 to 60 who are tired or stressed after work or study and comfortable with technology. Three findings from the earlier research shaped the features:

What participants saidWhat I designed
Relaxation spots are crowded, so full calm is hardA live crowd capacity screen
Some people want lights only at nightLight control with an on/off switch, and a dark interface suited to night use
Loud music disturbs other visitorsEarbud listening connected through the app

Divergent thinking: ideas I kept and dropped

I generated many ideas, then chose with feasibility, ethics and the brief in mind.

IdeaOutcomeWhy
Blue, water-themed appChanged to greenMatches the nature-inspired fountain and its calm
Fountain works only when music playsAny feature works aloneGives the user full control
Booking system to avoid queuingParked for laterCore controls came first
Virtual collaboration with friends and familyParked for laterNot essential to the brief
Heart rate and biometric dataRejectedPrivacy and ethics
AR animals and birdsRejectedToo dependent on device specifications
Seasonal app themesRejectedWould limit full personalisation
Fountain galleryRejectedOff topic

User flows

The first flow is a simple path from scanning the QR code through onboarding and sign-up to a home screen that branches to each feature. I then reworked it into a branching flow with decision points for each feature: locations, on/off, notifications, crowd capacity, mood themes, flow patterns, music with earbuds, meditation and light control.

Design decisions

Hick’s LawNavigation reduced to three elements, so choosing is quick.
Jakob’s LawHome, profile and play buttons sit where people expect them.
Fitts’s LawLarge containers on the home screen make targets easy to hit.
Tesler’s LawMusic and light screens stay complex because the controls are essential.
Common region and proximityMood themes share one gradient region, and related home controls sit together.
60-30-10 colour ruleDark grey 60%, a second grey 30%, and green or blue as the 10% call to action. Blue marks the meditation screen to signal mindfulness.
Dark modeChosen because the lights work best at night, with accessibility in mind.
Grid and structureAn 8-pixel grid with auto-layout. An on/off toggle replaced the scanner in the navigation so the fountain can be switched at any time.

Iteration

Onboarding colour

I started with a blue, watery theme, then moved to a green button, a green illustration, a clearer droplet on white, and finally dark mode, which suits the night-time light controls.

Home layout

Six layouts. The first had five navigation icons. The second added featured content, which pushed the location down and hid it. The third used squares and hid the fountain controls, which went against proximity. The fourth put the QR code bottom centre and looked untidy. The final layout combines the first and third with auto-layout and the 8-pixel grid.

Back button

Onboarding needed a way back, so I replaced the single large button with a medium button plus a Back button.

The final screens

Reflection and next steps

  • The app builds on the interviews I ran for the group fountain; I did not run new interviews for the app itself.
  • The prototype is not fully interactive, and some flows are unfinished.
  • It has not been usability tested. Next I would test the controls with people at a real fountain.
  • I would define how crowd capacity is measured, and review privacy for location and Bluetooth.
  • Parked ideas, such as booking, would come after the core controls are proven.

Illustrations from Storyset and icons from Icons8. Album art and photos are placeholder content.

Before you pay: verified volunteers against rental scams

A service that lets international students book a verified university volunteer to view a room for them, before they send a deposit from abroad.

MSc coursework, Edinburgh Napier University (Design Dialogues), 2023. Individual project. Methods: semi-structured interviews, affinity mapping, user stories, personas, conceptual and concrete scenarios with PACT analysis, requirements and sketching. Participants gave written consent and are anonymised here.

The problem

International students often have to secure a room in Edinburgh before they arrive. Rooms are scarce, so landlords ask for a deposit up front, sometimes before anyone has seen the place. After paying for tuition, visas and flights, a scam can leave a student with no money and nowhere to live in a country where they know no one.

I was an international student in Edinburgh myself, so I set out to learn how students deal with this and whether people who already live here could help.

Research

I ran semi-structured interviews with international students, local students and potential volunteers, mostly at Edinburgh Napier University and aged 17 to 40. Students were asked how they found their first room, whether they had paid a deposit unseen and what they feared. Potential volunteers were asked about their time, their knowledge of the housing market and how they would spot a fake listing.

What people said

Scams are close to home“A friend got scammed 250 pounds and was stuck in Edinburgh when he arrived.”
Unfamiliar ground“This is not our country. We don’t know what’s happening here.”
Photos are not enoughPhotos in an advert might not give a clear idea of the space, so a viewing is a must to confirm it is genuine.
Help is worth paying for“Even if I have to reimburse a volunteer, it’s better than coming here and having no room.”

Findings that shaped the design

FindingDesign response
Students fear paying a deposit for a room they have not seen, and several knew someone who had been scammedA volunteer views the room and reports back before any money is sent
Students accepted the idea, but wanted the volunteer to be verified, ideally by the universitySign-in through the university: a CAS number for incoming students, a university ID for volunteers
Everyone liked the idea of volunteering, but many had little free timeAn availability setting, so volunteers only receive requests when they can help
Students prefer someone from their course or who speaks their languageVolunteer cards with course, languages, experience and ratings, plus filters
Volunteers knew what to check: rent, bills, transport, flatmates and the termsA shared checklist for viewings, and notes and photos in the report
Some volunteers would help for free, but a small reward was welcomeRewards from the university or the student, and a rating system

Two users, two sides of the service

From the interviews I built two personas: Sarah, an incoming student who cannot view rooms from abroad, and Lara, a student who has lived in Edinburgh for a year and wants to pass on what she has learned.

Scenarios and requirements

Two concrete scenarios, written with PACT analysis, turned the personas into steps. In the first, Sarah signs in from abroad with her CAS number, filters volunteers by course and language, and sends a request. In the second, Lara accepts on her phone, checks the advert against public property records, views the room and reports back, and only then does Sarah pay.

Must haveNice to have
University sign-in and verificationVideo viewing, so the student can join the visit live
In-app messaging between student and volunteerA deposit hold, where the platform keeps the deposit until the student arrives
Matching students with available volunteersRatings, rewards and testimonials
Emergency support for volunteers out on viewingsA mobile app as well as a responsive website

Sketches

I sketched a dashboard website that could sit inside the university site.

Reflection and next steps

  • The concept has not been tested. Next I would run a usability test of the booking flow with incoming international students.
  • The sketches are desktop only. Most students would book from a phone, so the next step is a mobile flow.
  • More international students in the sample would strengthen the findings, as many participants on the interview day were local.
  • The deposit hold needs real thought about trust, payments and regulation before it could work.

About

I’m a UX designer with an MSc in User Experience Design from Edinburgh Napier University and a BA in Animation and Graphic Design. I care about interfaces that hold up outside the studio.

My story

I grew up in the UAE, trained in animation and graphic design in India, then moved to Edinburgh for an MSc in User Experience Design. Living across three countries has made me used to adapting to new places and people. Alongside and after my studies I worked on the front line of logistics, at Subway, in food delivery, at Parcelforce and as an agency driver for Royal Mail, with nearly a year as a graphic designer in between.

Doing the work showed me how often software ignores the people who use it in the rain, at speed and under pressure. That is the gap I want to design for.

Outside design, I restored my father’s 35-year-old motorcycle, the one I rode on as a baby in our old family photos. It took a year of working alongside a mechanic, and it taught me patience and how things really work. When I’m not designing, I’m travelling or watching football as a Barça fan.

How I work

1. Start where the work happensI watch real tasks in real conditions, through field observation, contextual inquiry and think-aloud sessions.
2. Name the problem preciselyI break tasks down and map friction to usability principles, so fixes target causes, not symptoms.
3. Design for the worst conditionsGloves, glare, one free hand and hidden settings. If it works there, it works everywhere.
4. Be honest about evidenceI label projections as projections, state the limits of my studies and plan how to test next.

What I’m looking for

UX or product design roles where real-world conditions matter, especially in logistics, mobility and enterprise tools.
